strengths: SFTMix addresses a relevant NLP problem with a straightforward adaptation of Mixup to autoregressive instruction tuning. Confidence-based pairing and interpolation of final hidden states and targets provide a concrete recipe that requires no additional human annotation.

Tables 1–2 show consistently positive comparisons against NTP across two model families and three training datasets. Overall MT-Bench gains are approximately 0.20–0.29 points, while average medical QA accuracy improves by 1.33 and 1.66 percentage points for Llama and Mistral, respectively.

The evaluation combines conversational benchmarks, length-controlled AlpacaEval scores, medical QA, and human preferences. The human study provides supporting evidence: among 200 judgments over 80 prompts, SFTMix receives 42.5% wins versus 26.5% for NTP, with 31% ties.

Experiments with a smaller reference model, data selection, LoRA, and alternative loss weights provide useful evidence of compatibility. The pipeline and core construction are understandable, and several important optimization settings are reported.
weaknesses: The central contribution of confidence-based pairing is not isolated. There is no otherwise identical random-pairing Mixup baseline, within-confidence pairing control, or comparison against confidence from a single checkpoint. Section 5.2 changes the response dataset when examining quality-based pairing but does not evaluate confidence-based pairing on that same modified dataset. Consequently, it cannot establish that training dynamics are crucial. Comparisons with the cited cartography-based Mixup work and instruction-tuning regularizers such as NEFTune would also clarify the contribution beyond existing methods.

The proposed mechanism exceeds the evidence. A t-SNE visualization of confidence extremes and inspection of 100 examples do not demonstrate that confident examples overfit more, or that SFTMix improves generalization specifically for unconfident examples. Perplexity can reflect response predictability, topic, formatting, and label noise. Appendix A establishes that the additional term changes gradients, but does not establish reduced overfitting or improved generalization. These claims need subgroup-specific held-out evidence or more cautious wording.

Evaluation uncertainty and model selection remain concerns. Five evaluation rounds do not establish variability across independently trained models, and no training-seed variation, confidence intervals, or significance tests accompany the modest improvements. Appendix B.1 selects the regularization weight using MT-Bench and AlpacaEval-2, which also supply headline results, without identifying a separate development set. The human study omits annotator counts, assignment and ordering procedures, agreement, and uncertainty accounting for repeated judgments of the same prompts.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the core recipe being understandable. The manuscript provides no implementation link and omits reference-checkpoint timing, sequence-length and prompt settings, LoRA configuration, and exact judge and generation settings. The loss notation also places a negative sign before a quantity called cross-entropy, whereas Appendix A differentiates conventional positive cross-entropy; this appears to be a correctable notation error. Together with the missing component controls and uncertainty estimates, these gaps prevent a clear Findings recommendation.

The practical cost-benefit case is underdeveloped. The default procedure requires an additional reference-model fine-tuning run and checkpoint-based dataset scoring, but reports no total runtime, memory, or compute comparison. Smaller-reference and LoRA experiments demonstrate feasibility in selected settings, while leaving the claimed scalability and suitability for compute-constrained use insufficiently quantified.
